subject: Events service — datastore choice for v2
body:
Hi Rohan, Devika,

As we plan v2 of the Events Service, want to align early on datastore. From product side I care about (a) audit-grade durability, (b) flexible querying for analytics dashboards, (c) ability to keep up with growth — Hooli alone is projected to push 5x current event volume by EOY.

A few of the team have been suggesting MongoDB. Curious where you're landing.

Diego

subject: Re: Events service — datastore choice for v2
body:
Going to push back on Mongo before we even start.

Three reasons:

1. The events table needs strong joins against `users` and `subscriptions`. Both live in Postgres. Putting events in Mongo guarantees we'll either denormalize (now Mongo is your ETL target, fun) or paper over it with application-side joins (slow + bug-prone). Boring solution: keep events in Postgres next to its relations.

2. We already paid the cost of moving billing OFF Mongo in 2022. Tarun has the scars. There's no version of 'this time it'll be different' I believe.

3. 5x current volume is roughly 25M events/day. Postgres handles that with appropriate partitioning. If it gets to 50M+/day, ClickHouse becomes the right answer — not Mongo.

Will write up an RFC. Diego — to your audit/durability point: Postgres + WAL replication is a stronger story for compliance customers (Umbrella, Oscorp) than Mongo's replication story.

Proposing the RFC review for Sept 14.

—r

title: RFC: Events store — Q3 2023
author: Rohan Iyer
body:
## TL;DR
Keep events in Postgres. Add monthly time-based partitioning, dedicated read replica, async export pipeline for analytics. Re-evaluate ClickHouse if event volume crosses 50M/day sustained.

## Context
Events Service v2 needs a datastore decision. Today we use the same Postgres cluster as the rest of platform, with no partitioning. Performance is fine but won't scale to projected volumes.

## Options considered

### Option A — Postgres (recommended)
- Time-partitioned `events` table, monthly partitions, attach/detach for retention.
- Read replica dedicated to analytical queries.
- Async export to ClickHouse staging for heavy aggregation use cases (later).
- Pros: relational joins to users/subscriptions stay native. Operational story is one we already run. Audit/compliance story is strong (WAL replication, point-in-time recovery).
- Cons: write throughput will eventually become the bottleneck. We have ~3 years of headroom before 50M/day.

### Option B — MongoDB
- Single events collection, sharded.
- Pros: schema flexibility for evolving event payloads.
- Cons: relational joins to Postgres-resident user/subscription data become application logic, which is the bug surface we just removed in 2022 with the billing migration off Mongo. Replication semantics under partition are weaker than Postgres for compliance customers.
- Verdict: rejected. Schema flexibility is achievable in Postgres via `JSONB` columns without taking on a separate operational footprint.

### Option C — ClickHouse
- Columnar store, built for analytical workloads.
- Pros: best-in-class for the query patterns the analytics dashboards want.
- Cons: no transactional joins. Operationally new (no team experience). Adds a second store of record.
- Verdict: deferred. Not the right answer at current volume. Re-evaluate at 50M events/day.

## Decision
Option A. Re-evaluation trigger: sustained 50M events/day OR analytical query latency p99 > 5s on the read replica.

## Rollback
Partitioning is non-destructive. If we change our mind on partitioning strategy, we re-attach. If we change datastore entirely, we'd dual-write for a quarter, then cut over — same playbook as the 2022 billing-off-Mongo migration.

## Open questions
- Retention policy for partitions — Diego, what's the product position on customer-facing event history? Currently unbounded.
- Compliance review — Sasha to weigh in on PITR for HIPAA-adjacent customers (Umbrella).

title: Architecture review — Events store RFC
discussion:
Rohan walked through the RFC. Diego pressed on schema flexibility for new event types — Rohan demonstrated JSONB pattern with a partial index example. Tarun reinforced the Mongo migration history. Sasha confirmed Postgres PITR meets Umbrella's compliance needs.

Maya raised the 50M/day trigger — pushed for adding 'analytical query latency p99 > 5s on read replica' as an alternate trigger. Rohan agreed; updated in RFC.

Tarun asked about retention. Diego said product position is bounded retention (1 year customer-facing, longer for internal forensics). Rohan to spec retention partition rotation in follow-up.
decisions: Approve Option A (Postgres with monthly time-partitioning + dedicated read replica + async ClickHouse staging export, future)
Re-evaluation triggers: 50M events/day sustained OR analytical p99 > 5s
Retention: 1 year customer-facing, 3 years internal — partition detach pattern

action_items.item: Update RFC with Maya's alt trigger and retention spec

title: ADR-0017: Events service uses Postgres with monthly time-partitioning
author: Rohan Iyer
body:
## Status
Accepted — 2023-09-14 architecture review.

## Context
Events service v2 datastore selection. See RFC: Events store — Q3 2023.

## Decision
Use Postgres with monthly time-partitioned `events` table and a dedicated analytics read replica. JSONB for variable event payloads.

## Consequences
+ Joins against users/subscriptions stay native.
+ Operational footprint stays unified.
+ Compliance story (PITR, WAL) preserved for HIPAA-adjacent customers.
- Write throughput ceiling around 50M events/day; revisit when approaching.
- ClickHouse remains the planned future destination for heavy analytics, not Mongo.

## Re-evaluation triggers
- Sustained 50M events/day OR
- Analytical query latency p99 > 5s on the read replica.

subject: Events volume — we're approaching the trigger
body:
Last 30 days — Hooli + Globex pushed us to 42M/day average, peak day was 47M. We're not at 50M yet but the trajectory says we'll be sustained over by Q3.

Want to revive the ClickHouse conversation per ADR-0017. I can spike a side-by-side for the heaviest analytical query (the 90-day per-tenant aggregation) and report back.

Tarun

subject: Re: Events volume — we're approaching the trigger
body:
+1 to spike. Three-week box. Scope:

1. Stand up CH in a non-prod env, dual-write last 30 days of events.
2. Run the 90-day per-tenant aggregation on both. Compare p50, p95, p99, cost, ops complexity.
3. Decision matrix — if CH is < 5x faster, we don't switch yet. If 5x+, write the migration plan.

FTR: I want to be honest with ourselves about whether this is the trigger or just the first signal. The honest version of the trigger is 'we can't keep up without unhappy queries' — measure that, not the volume number alone.

—r

title: Spike report — ClickHouse for Events analytics
author: Tarun Kapoor
body:
## TL;DR
ClickHouse is faster for the analytical workload (3.4x p95 on the 90-day per-tenant aggregation), but not enough to justify the operational addition right now. Postgres read replica still meets SLA. **Recommend: defer migration. Re-spike when sustained 60M/day OR replica p95 exceeds 8s on aggregation queries.**

## Setup
Dual-wrote events for 30 days into a CH cluster (3 nodes, 16 vCPU each). MergeTree engine, partitioning by toYYYYMM(timestamp).

## Results
| Query | Postgres replica p95 | ClickHouse p95 | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 90-day per-tenant agg | 4.2s | 1.2s | 3.5x |
| 30-day rollup | 1.1s | 0.4s | 2.7x |
| Live last-1h tail | 180ms | 110ms | 1.6x |

Write throughput: CH peaked at 320k events/sec (vs Postgres 85k). Not the bottleneck right now.

## Operational delta
- New cluster, new ops runbooks, new on-call training.
- Backup/restore patterns different.
- Integration with current ETL: another sink.

## Decision matrix
Rohan's gate from email: 5x+ p95 speedup to migrate. We hit 3.5x. Below threshold.

## Recommendation
Defer. Document spike findings (this doc). Set new triggers:
- Sustained 60M events/day, OR
- Replica p95 > 8s on aggregation queries.

## Cost not migrating
We will revisit. Probably 12-18 months out at current trajectory. The team has the runway.
